description:
Total depravity is explained as corruption affecting every faculty and moral inability to come to God without grace. Introducing the TULIP study, Wesam Saad connects the doctrine with God’s sovereignty, trust and worship, while acknowledging that godly Christians may disagree with this theology. He distinguishes total corruption from being as wicked as possible and does not deny outwardly good actions by unbelievers. Passages about the mind, affections and will establish the breadth of his argument. The discussion then follows Jesus’ statements about new birth and the Father’s drawing, alongside passages describing inability to please God or receive spiritual truth.

Saad clarifies that this inability is moral rather than the absence of human faculties. People possess minds, wills and affections, but he argues that their desires are opposed to God. The language of spiritual death and the deceitful heart is used to explain dependence on divine grace without removing accountability. A question about believers brings his distinction between the new heart and remaining sin in the flesh. The concluding applications challenge confidence in self-salvation and encourage perseverance in evangelism. Outward differences between people should not determine hope, and reliance on God is expressly joined with care and accuracy in presenting the gospel.

questions.question: Why does Saad consider the TULIP study important?
questions.answer: He connects its themes with God’s sovereignty, the understanding of salvation, trust and worship. He also explicitly says that embracing TULIP is not a condition for being a Christian or belonging to the church. The study is presented as a defended theological position, with the godliness of some who disagree acknowledged.

questions.question: What does “total” mean, and what does it not mean?
questions.answer: Saad uses it to mean that every faculty is affected by sin, including the mind, affections and will. He does not mean that everyone is equally wicked or as bad as possible. Nor does he deny that unbelievers can perform outwardly good actions; his central concern is their relation to God and inability to save themselves.

questions.question: How are the mind, affections and will brought into the argument?
questions.answer: Saad places together the hostile mind, love of darkness and the absence of seeking God. He reads these as describing the reach of sin throughout the person rather than a defect in only one area. The combined passages support his account of moral corruption as comprehensive.

questions.question: How does he understand the order of new birth, drawing and coming to Christ?
questions.answer: He reads the inability statements as requiring God’s action before the person can see, enter or come. In his exposition, new birth enables sight of the kingdom, and the Father’s drawing precedes coming to Christ. The source presents this causal order as central to dependence on grace.

questions.question: Why does he emphasise spiritual death rather than mere sickness?
questions.answer: Saad uses the contrast to deny that a person can independently supply the decisive response once a little help is offered. The death imagery describes inability in relation to God, not physical inactivity. When he considers sickness imagery, he insists that it must include the person’s opposition to the very help needed.

questions.question: How can inability and accountability belong together in his explanation?
questions.answer: Saad distinguishes possessing human faculties from desiring to use them towards God. He argues that the inability under discussion arises from moral opposition rather than the absence of a mind, will or affections. This is why he rejects the comparison with being commanded to fly without wings and retains human accountability.

questions.question: How does Saad distinguish believers from the condition being described?
questions.answer: He says that regeneration replaces the old heart with a new heart aligned with God, while sin still remains in the flesh. He expressly acknowledges continuing corruption in the flesh, so his distinction is not a claim of whole-person sinlessness.

questions.question: What warning does the doctrine give against postponing salvation?
questions.answer: Saad challenges the idea that someone can indulge sin and later activate salvation at will. In his argument, recognition of inability should break self-reliance and lead a person to seek Christ’s mercy. The application is dependence on grace, rather than confidence in controlling the timing and outcome of conversion.

questions.question: How does this teaching shape his approach to evangelism?
questions.answer: Saad argues that outwardly different people share the same need for God’s saving action, so a difficult response should not quickly extinguish hope. He encourages continued gospel witness and growth through mistakes. He expressly rejects careless presentation, joining reliance on God with an effort to communicate accurately.
